title: Δῶρα καὶ οἰωνός
titleEn: Farewell Gifts and an Omen — Odyssey 15.86–171
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Telemachus tells Menelaus that he wants to go home at once: he left no one to guard his property, and he fears for it while he searches for his father. Menelaus has a meal prepared and goes to his store-room with Helen and his son Megapenthes. He gives Telemachus a double cup and a silver mixing-bowl that Hephaestus made, and Helen gives him a robe, for his future wife to wear. After a last meal the two young men yoke their horses and drive out. As they go, Menelaus comes after them with a cup of wine and sends them off with a message for Nestor. Telemachus answers that they will tell Nestor everything. Then an eagle flies up on the right with a tame goose in its talons, and the crowd runs after it shouting. Peisistratus asks Menelaus whether the omen was sent to the two of them or to him, and while Menelaus is still thinking, Helen speaks first.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: This is the fixed formula that introduces Telemachus's replies. τόν is the pronoun 'him', here Menelaus, whose offer of a journey and of parting gifts closed the previous part. αὖ 'in turn' marks a new speaker, and πεπνυμένος 'prudent' is Telemachus's stock epithet, translated every time. ἀντίον is an adverb, 'facing, face to face', and ηὔδα is the imperfect of αὐδάω 'speak'.

sentences.t:
Ἀτρεΐδη Μενέλαε διοτρεφές, ὄρχαμε λαῶν,
βούλομαι ἤδη νεῖσθαι ἐφ’ ἡμέτερ’·
sentences.tr:
Atreïdē Menelae diotrephes, orchame laōn,
boulomai ēdē neisthai eph’ hēmeter’·
sentences.l:
“Atreus' son, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, chief of the people,
I wish now to go to what is ours;
sentences.i: “Son of Atreus, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, chief of the people, I wish to go home now;
sentences.n: Telemachus opens with the full form of address, a string of vocatives: Ἀτρεΐδη 'son of Atreus', the name, διοτρεφές 'Zeus-nurtured' and ὄρχαμε λαῶν 'chief of the people'. Each is translated every time it comes. βούλομαι ἤδη νεῖσθαι is 'I wish now to go', with νεῖσθαι the infinitive of νέομαι 'go, return'. ἐφ’ is ἐπί with its vowel elided and its π turned to φ by the rough breathing of the next word, and ἡμέτερ’ is the neuter plural ἡμέτερα 'our things' with its noun left out; beside νεῖσθαι the sense is 'to my own place', that is, home. The unit ends at the ano teleia in mid-line, because οὐ γάρ opens the reason.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ὄπισθεν
οὖρον ἰὼν κατέλειπον ἐπὶ κτεάτεσσιν ἐμοῖσιν·
sentences.tr:
ou gar opisthen
ouron iōn kateleipon epi kteatessin emoisin·
sentences.l:
for not behind
a warden, going, was I leaving over my possessions;
sentences.i: for when I set out I left no warden behind to watch over my possessions;
sentences.n: οὖρον is the accusative of οὖρος 'warden, guardian', a different word from οὖρος 'fair wind' although it is spelled the same; the sense is fixed by κατέλειπον ἐπὶ κτεάτεσσιν 'I was leaving behind over my possessions', which could not be said of a wind. ὄπισθεν is 'behind', and ἰών is the participle of εἶμι 'go', here 'as I went away'. κτεάτεσσιν is the dative plural of κτέατα 'possessions' with the ending -εσσι(ν), and ἐμοῖσιν is the matching dative of ἐμός with -οισι(ν). γάρ gives the reason for wanting to leave at once.

sentences.t:
μὴ πατέρ’ ἀντίθεον διζήμενος αὐτὸς ὄλωμαι,
ἤ τί μοι ἐκ μεγάρων κειμήλιον ἐσθλὸν ὄληται.
sentences.tr:
mē pater’ antitheon dizēmenos autos olōmai,
ē ti moi ek megarōn keimēlion esthlon olētai.
sentences.l:
lest, seeking my godlike father, I myself perish,
or some good treasure of mine from the halls perish.”
sentences.i: lest, while I search for my godlike father, I myself perish, or some good treasure be lost from my halls.”
sentences.n: μή with the subjunctive ὄλωμαι is 'lest I perish', a clause of fear that depends on the wish to go home. The second clause, joined by ἤ 'or' (accented, not ἦ 'truly'), is governed by the same μή, and its subject is the treasure. ὄλωμαι and ὄληται are subjunctives of the same verb ὄλλυμι: 'perish' of a man, 'be lost' of a thing. διζήμενος is the participle of δίζημαι 'seek'. ἀντίθεον 'godlike' is Odysseus's epithet, standing in place of his name, which Telemachus does not use. κειμήλιον 'treasure' is a thing laid up, from the root of κεῖμαι 'lie'. μεγάρων is a plural for one house, and ἐσθλόν is 'good'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ τό γ’ ἄκουσε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος,
αὐτίκ’ ἄρ’ ᾗ ἀλόχῳ ἠδὲ δμῳῇσι κέλευσε
δεῖπνον ἐνὶ μεγάροις τετυκεῖν ἅλις ἔνδον ἐόντων.
sentences.tr:
autar epei to g’ akouse boēn agathos Menelaos,
autik’ ar’ hēi alochōi ēde dmōiēisi keleuse
deipnon eni megarois tetykein halis endon eontōn.
sentences.l:
But when that he heard, Menelaus, good at the war-cry,
at once then to his own wife and to the maidservants he gave orders
a meal in the halls to prepare, enough from what is within.
sentences.i: And when Menelaus, good at the war-cry, heard this, he at once told his wife and the maidservants to prepare a meal in the halls, enough from what was in the house.
sentences.n: βοὴν ἀγαθός is Menelaus's stock epithet, 'good at the war-cry': βοήν is an accusative of respect, the battle-shout, and the phrase is translated every time. τό γε is 'that', and ἄκουσε is an unaugmented aorist. ᾗ ἀλόχῳ: ᾗ is the possessive 'his own', in the dative, not a relative, and ἀλόχῳ ἠδὲ δμῳῇσι is 'to his wife and the maidservants' (δμῳῇσι is the dative plural of δμῳή 'maidservant'). κέλευσε takes a dative of the persons and an infinitive, τετυκεῖν, the aorist infinitive of τεύχω 'make ready'. ἅλις is 'enough', and ἔνδον ἐόντων is a partitive genitive, 'of what was within'. The last line is the order Menelaus announced in his speech in the previous part, now given.

sentences.t:
ἀγχίμολον δέ οἱ ἦλθε Βοηθοΐδης Ἐτεωνεύς,
ἀνστὰς ἐξ εὐνῆς, ἐπεὶ οὐ πολὺ ναῖεν ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ·
sentences.tr:
anchimolon de hoi ēlthe Boēthoïdēs Eteōneus,
anstas ex eunēs, epei ou poly naien ap’ autou·
sentences.l:
And close by him came the son of Boethous, Eteoneus,
risen from bed, since not far did he dwell from him;
sentences.i: Close by him came Eteoneus, son of Boethous, who had risen from his bed, for he did not live far from him;
sentences.n: ἀγχίμολον is an adverb, 'close by'; οἱ is the enclitic dative 'to him', Menelaus. Βοηθοΐδης is a patronymic, 'son of Boethous', with the ending -ίδης, and it stands beside the man's own name, Ἐτεωνεύς. ἀνστάς is the aorist participle of ἀνίστημι, 'having risen' (Attic ἀναστάς), and ἐξ εὐνῆς is 'from bed'. ναῖεν is the imperfect of ναίω 'dwell', without the augment; οὐ πολύ is 'not far', and ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ is 'from him'. The clause explains why he could come so quickly.

sentences.t:
τὸν πῦρ κῆαι ἄνωγε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Μενέλαος
ὀπτῆσαί τε κρεῶν·
sentences.tr:
ton pyr kēai anōge boēn agathos Menelaos
optēsai te kreōn·
sentences.l:
Him to kindle fire he bade, Menelaus, good at the war-cry,
and to roast some of the meat;
sentences.i: Menelaus, good at the war-cry, told him to kindle a fire and roast some of the meat;
sentences.n: τόν is Eteoneus, the object of ἄνωγε. ἄνωγε comes from ἄνωγα, a perfect with present sense 'I bid, order'; here, in narrative, it is 'he bade'. πῦρ κῆαι is 'to kindle fire': κῆαι is the epic aorist infinitive of καίω 'burn, light'. ὀπτῆσαι is the aorist infinitive of ὀπτάω 'roast', and κρεῶν is a partitive genitive, 'some of the meat' (Attic κρεῶν, genitive plural of κρέας). The same epithet βοὴν ἀγαθός comes back, translated the same way.

sentences.t: ὁ δ’ ἄρ’ οὐκ ἀπίθησεν ἀκούσας.
sentences.tr: ho d’ ar’ ouk apithēsen akousas.
sentences.l: and he, then, did not disobey, having heard.
sentences.i: and he did not disobey when he heard.
sentences.n: οὐκ ἀπίθησεν 'did not disobey' is a litotes, a denial of the opposite: Eteoneus obeyed at once. ἀπίθησεν is the aorist of ἀπιθέω, and ἀκούσας is the aorist participle 'having heard', here 'on hearing'. ὁ δ’ ἄρ’ is 'and he then', with ὁ the pronoun.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’ ἐς θάλαμον κατεβήσετο κηώεντα,
οὐκ οἶος, ἅμα τῷ γ’ Ἑλένη κίε καὶ Μεγαπένθης.
sentences.tr:
autos d’ es thalamon katebēseto kēōenta,
ouk oios, hama tōi g’ Helenē kie kai Megapenthēs.
sentences.l:
And himself into the fragrant chamber went down,
not alone; with him Helen went, and Megapenthes.
sentences.i: He himself went down into the fragrant chamber, and he did not go alone: Helen went with him, and Megapenthes.
sentences.n: αὐτός 'himself' sets Menelaus against the household he has just given orders to. ἐς θάλαμον is 'into the chamber'; it is a store-room for valuables, as the treasures at 101 show. κατεβήσετο is an aorist middle of καταβαίνω 'go down', in the epic -σε- form. κηώεντα 'fragrant' is the traditional gloss. οὐκ οἶος is 'not alone', with the smooth breathing; οἷος with the rough breathing means 'such as'. κίε is 'went', from κίω, and ἅμα τῷ γε is 'along with him', τῷ being the pronoun. Megapenthes is named here for the first time in this part; line 103 says he is Menelaus's son.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἵκανον ὅθι κειμήλια κεῖτο,
Ἀτρεΐδης μὲν ἔπειτα δέπας λάβεν ἀμφικύπελλον,
υἱὸν δὲ κρητῆρα φέρειν Μεγαπένθε’ ἄνωγεν
ἀργύρεον·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē rh’ hikanon hothi keimēlia keito,
Atreïdēs men epeita depas laben amphikypellon,
huion de krētēra pherein Megapenthe’ anōgen
argyreon·
sentences.l:
But when indeed they came to where the treasures lay,
the son of Atreus then took a double cup,
and his son, the mixing-bowl to carry, Megapenthes, he bade,
of silver;
sentences.i: But when they reached the place where the treasures lay, the son of Atreus took a double cup, and told his son Megapenthes to carry a silver mixing-bowl;
sentences.n: ἵκανον is an unaugmented imperfect of ἱκάνω 'reach'. ὅθι 'where' has the suffix -θι of place. κειμήλια is a neuter plural but takes the singular κεῖτο 'lay' (also without augment), as neuter plurals regularly do; κειμήλια 'treasures' is the word of 91. Ἀτρεΐδης used alone is 'the son of Atreus'. δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον is the 'double cup'; whether ἀμφικύπελλον means 'double' or 'two-handled' is disputed, and the translation does not choose. λάβεν is the unaugmented aorist of λαμβάνω. υἱόν and the elided name Μεγαπένθε’ stand together as the object of ἄνωγεν 'bade', with φέρειν as its infinitive. A κρητήρ is the big bowl in which wine was mixed with water, and ἀργύρεον 'of silver', carried over the line-end, belongs to it. Line 101 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the scanner can fit it only by counting the last syllable of ὅθι long in the fourth foot, and it must also read the α of ἵκανον as long, which is not certain.

sentences.t:
Ἑλένη δὲ παρίστατο φωριαμοῖσιν,
ἔνθ’ ἔσαν οἱ πέπλοι παμποίκιλοι, οὓς κάμεν αὐτή.
sentences.tr:
Helenē de paristato phōriamoisin,
enth’ esan hoi peploi pampoikiloi, hous kamen autē.
sentences.l:
And Helen was standing beside the chests,
where were the robes, all-intricate, which she herself had made.
sentences.i: Helen stood beside the chests, where lay the robes of richly intricate work that she herself had made.
sentences.n: παρίστατο is the imperfect middle of παρίστημι 'stand beside', with the dative φωριαμοῖσιν 'chests', a dative plural in -οισι(ν) (φωριαμός is a rare word for a chest, here one that holds clothing). ἔσαν is the epic form of ἦσαν 'were'. οἱ may be the article 'the' with πέπλοι, as the word-for-word English takes it, or the dative 'for her' (the robes were hers); the picture is the same. πέπλος is a 'robe'. παμποίκιλοι is παν- 'all' with ποικίλος, 'intricately worked'. κάμεν is the unaugmented aorist of κάμνω 'toil', here 'work at, make'; οὓς κάμεν αὐτή says that Helen made these robes herself.

sentences.t:
τῶν ἕν’ ἀειραμένη Ἑλένη φέρε, δῖα γυναικῶν,
ὃς κάλλιστος ἔην ποικίλμασιν ἠδὲ μέγιστος,
ἀστὴρ δ’ ὣς ἀπέλαμπεν·
sentences.tr:
tōn hen’ aeiramenē Helenē phere, dia gynaikōn,
hos kallistos eēn poikilmasin ēde megistos,
astēr d’ hōs apelampen·
sentences.i: Helen, heavenly among women, lifted one of them out and carried it, the one that was the most beautiful in its intricate work and the largest, and it shone like a star;
sentences.n: τῶν ἕν’ is 'one of them', a partitive genitive with the accusative of ἕν’; ἀειραμένη is the aorist middle participle of ἀείρω 'lift', and φέρε is an unaugmented imperfect, 'was carrying'. δῖα γυναικῶν is Helen's epithet-phrase, translated every time: δῖα is 'heavenly' and γυναικῶν a partitive genitive 'among women'. ὅς is the relative, masculine to agree with the robe. ἔην is the epic form of ἦν, and ποικίλμασιν is a dative of respect from ποίκιλμα, a worked pattern, 'in its intricate work'. ἀστὴρ δ’ ὣς is 'and like a star': ὥς with the accent is 'like', here placed after its noun; ἀπέλαμπεν is 'shone out'.

sentences.t: ἔκειτο δὲ νείατος ἄλλων.
sentences.tr: ekeito de neiatos allōn.
sentences.l: and it lay lowest of the others.
sentences.i: and it lay at the bottom of the rest.
sentences.n: νείατος is a superlative, 'lowest, last'; of garments stacked in a chest it is 'undermost'. ἄλλων is a partitive genitive, 'of the others', after the superlative. ἔκειτο is the imperfect of κεῖμαι 'lie', and δέ adds a second fact about the same robe.

sentences.t:
βὰν δ’ ἰέναι προτέρω διὰ δώματος, ἧος ἵκοντο
Τηλέμαχον·
sentences.tr:
ban d’ ienai proterō dia dōmatos, hēos hikonto
Tēlemachon·
sentences.l:
And they set out to go farther through the house, until they reached
Telemachus;
sentences.i: They set out to go on through the house until they reached Telemachus;
sentences.n: βάν is the unaugmented aorist of βαίνω; with ἰέναι, the infinitive of εἶμι, it makes the formula 'set out to go' that opens a movement. προτέρω is 'farther on'. ἧος is the epic form of ἕως 'until', and ἵκοντο is an unaugmented aorist middle of ἱκνέομαι 'come to', with Τηλέμαχον as its object, at the head of the next line. The subject is the party that went down at 99–100.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ προσέφη ξανθὸς Μενέλαος·
sentences.tr: ton de prosephē xanthos Menelaos·
sentences.l: And him addressed fair-haired Menelaus:
sentences.i: And fair-haired Menelaus said to him:
sentences.n: τόν is the pronoun 'him', Telemachus. προσέφη is the aorist of πρόσφημι 'speak to', and 'addressed' is kept for this verb. Nothing has just been said to Menelaus (Telemachus's request is back at 87–91), so this is an opening and not a reply. ξανθός 'fair-haired' is Menelaus's stock epithet, translated every time.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχ’, ἦ τοι νόστον, ὅπως φρεσὶ σῇσι μενοινᾷς,
ὥς τοι Ζεὺς τελέσειεν, ἐρίγδουπος πόσις Ἥρης.
sentences.tr:
Tēlemach’, ē toi noston, hopōs phresi sēisi menoināis,
hōs toi Zeus teleseien, erigdoupos posis Hērēs.
sentences.l:
“Telemachus, truly the homecoming, as in your wits you desire it,
so may Zeus accomplish it for you, loud-crashing husband of Hera.
sentences.i: “Telemachus, truly may Zeus, the loud-crashing husband of Hera, bring your homecoming to pass for you, just as you desire it in your mind.
sentences.n: This is a wish, built on a correlation: ὅπως … ὥς 'as … so'. ἦ τοι is 'truly'. νόστον 'homecoming' is the object of τελέσειεν, held up to the front of the sentence; τελέσειεν is the aorist optative of τελέω 'bring to fulfilment', a wish for the future. μενοινᾷς is a contracted second singular of μενοινάω 'be bent on, long for', and φρεσὶ σῇσι is a dative plural in -ῃσι with σός 'your'. τοι in the second line is the dative 'for you'. ἐρίγδουπος 'loud-crashing' is Zeus's epithet, built on ἐρι- 'very' and δοῦπος 'heavy crash'; 'thundering' is only the traditional reading of it. πόσις Ἥρης is 'husband of Hera' (Ἥρης is the Ionic genitive).

sentences.t:
δώρων δ’, ὅσσ’ ἐν ἐμῷ οἴκῳ κειμήλια κεῖται,
δώσω ὃ κάλλιστον καὶ τιμηέστατόν ἐστι.
sentences.tr:
dōrōn d’, hoss’ en emōi oikōi keimēlia keitai,
dōsō ho kalliston kai timēestaton esti.
sentences.l:
But of the gifts, as many treasures as in my house lie stored,
I will give the one that is fairest and most honoured.
sentences.i: Of all the treasures stored up as gifts in my house, I will give you the one that is finest and most highly prized.
sentences.n: δώρων is a partitive genitive, 'of the gifts', and ὅσσ’ is 'as many as'. κειμήλια κεῖται is again a neuter plural with a singular verb, 'treasures lie stored'. ὃ is the relative 'the one that', a neuter, not the possessive; κάλλιστον and τιμηέστατον are superlatives, 'fairest' and 'most honoured' (τιμήεις is 'honoured, prized'). These two lines also stand in Menelaus's offer at 4.613–614, except that the second there ends ἐστιν· and here ἐστι., and the English of that passage is kept.

sentences.t: δώσω τοι κρητῆρα τετυγμένον·
sentences.tr: dōsō toi krētēra tetygmenon·
sentences.l: I will give you a wrought mixing-bowl;
sentences.i: I will give you a well-wrought mixing-bowl;
sentences.n: τετυγμένον is the perfect passive participle of τεύχω 'make', 'wrought'; it is the word for a thing of fine craftsmanship, and the readable English keeps that sense. τοι is the dative 'you'. The ano teleia ends the unit, and the description of the bowl follows.

sentences.t:
ἀργύρεος δὲ
ἐστὶν ἅπας, χρυσῷ δ’ ἐπὶ χείλεα κεκράανται,
ἔργον δ’ Ἡφαίστοιο·
sentences.tr:
argyreos de
estin hapas, chrysōi d’ epi cheilea kekraantai,
ergon d’ Hēphaistoio·
sentences.i: it is entirely silver, its rims finished with gold, the work of Hephaestus;
sentences.n: ἀργύρεος is 'of silver', and ἅπας is 'all, entire'. χείλεα are 'lips', the rims of the bowl. κεκράανται is the perfect passive, third plural, of a verb meaning 'accomplish, finish'; 'finished with gold' is the sense the context gives, the verb being rare. ἐπί is a preverb standing apart from its verb. ἔργον Ἡφαίστοιο is 'the work of Hephaestus', the craftsman god, so a mark of the finest workmanship. These lines also stand at 4.615–617, there with ἔστιν for ἐστίν, and the English of that passage is kept.

sentences.t:
πόρεν δέ ἑ Φαίδιμος ἥρως,
Σιδονίων βασιλεύς, ὅθ’ ἑὸς δόμος ἀμφεκάλυψε
κεῖσέ με νοστήσαντα·
sentences.tr:
poren de he Phaidimos hērōs,
Sidoniōn basileus, hoth’ heos domos amphekalypse
keise me nostēsanta·
sentences.i: Phaedimus the hero, king of the Sidonians, gave it to me, when his own house sheltered me there on my journey home;
sentences.n: πόρεν is the unaugmented aorist of πόρω 'give, grant', and ἑ is the pronoun 'it', the bowl. Φαίδιμος is here a person's name, the same word as the adjective 'glorious'; ἥρως is 'hero' used as a title, and Σιδονίων βασιλεύς is 'king of the Sidonians', the people of Sidon. ὅθ’ is ὅτε 'when', and ἑὸς δόμος is 'his own house': ἑός is the possessive 'his own'. ἀμφεκάλυψε is the aorist of ἀμφικαλύπτω 'cover round, shelter'. κεῖσε is 'to that place', and με νοστήσαντα is 'me having come home', that is, on my way home.

sentences.t: τεῒν δ’ ἐθέλω τόδ’ ὀπάσσαι.
sentences.tr: teïn d’ ethelō tod’ opassai.
sentences.l: and to you I wish to give this.”
sentences.i: and now I want to give it to you.”
sentences.n: τεΐν is the epic dative of σύ, 'to you' (Attic σοί); Murray prints it τεῒν before δ’. ἐθέλω is 'I wish, am willing', and ὀπάσσαι is the aorist infinitive of ὀπάζω 'bestow, grant'. τόδε points to the bowl. The closing quotation mark ends Menelaus's speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ἐν χειρὶ τίθει δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον
ἥρως Ἀτρεΐδης·
sentences.tr:
hōs eipōn en cheiri tithei depas amphikypellon
hērōs Atreïdēs·
sentences.l:
So having spoken, in his hand he placed the double cup,
the hero, the son of Atreus;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the hero, the son of Atreus, placed the double cup in his hand;
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών is 'so having spoken', the masculine aorist participle of the formula whose feminine comes at 130. ἐν χειρί is 'in the hand', and τίθει is the unaugmented imperfect of τίθημι, 'placed'. The Greek does not name the receiver, who is Telemachus. ἥρως 'hero' and Ἀτρεΐδης 'the son of Atreus' are both kept, each translated every time. δέπας ἀμφικύπελλον is the 'double cup' of 102, the same words.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἄρα κρητῆρα φαεινὸν
θῆκ’ αὐτοῦ προπάροιθε φέρων κρατερὸς Μεγαπένθης,
ἀργύρεον·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ara krētēra phaeinon
thēk’ autou proparoithe pherōn krateros Megapenthēs,
argyreon·
sentences.i: and strong Megapenthes brought the shining mixing-bowl and set it down in front of him, a bowl of silver;
sentences.n: ὁ δ’ ἄρα is 'and he then', with ὁ the pronoun that the name Μεγαπένθης, at the end of the next line, explains. φαεινός is 'shining'. θῆκ’ is the unaugmented aorist θῆκε of τίθημι. αὐτοῦ is most simply the genitive 'him' with προπάροιθε 'in front of'; it could also be the adverb 'right there', and either way the bowl is set down before Telemachus. κρατερός 'strong' is Megapenthes's epithet, translated every time. ἀργύρεον 'of silver' again waits at the head of the next line, as at 104.

sentences.t:
Ἑλένη δὲ παρίστατο καλλιπάρῃος
πέπλον ἔχουσ’ ἐν χερσίν, ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε·
sentences.tr:
Helenē de paristato kalliparēios
peplon echous’ en chersin, epos t’ ephat’ ek t’ onomaze·
sentences.l:
and Helen was standing beside, fair-cheeked,
holding the robe in her hands, and spoke a word and called him by name:
sentences.i: Helen, fair-cheeked, stood beside him with the robe in her hands, and spoke, calling him by name:
sentences.n: παρίστατο is 'was standing beside', as at 104. καλλιπάρῃος is 'fair-cheeked': παρῃά is 'cheek', and καλλι- is 'fair'; it is Helen's epithet here, translated every time. ἔχουσ’ is the participle 'holding', and χερσίν is a dative plural. ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε is the formula of a personal address: ἐκ … ὀνόμαζε is tmesis for ἐξονομάζω, 'speak out by name'. The speech that follows is Helen's.

sentences.t:
δῶρόν τοι καὶ ἐγώ, τέκνον φίλε, τοῦτο δίδωμι,
μνῆμ’ Ἑλένης χειρῶν, πολυηράτου ἐς γάμου ὥρην,
σῇ ἀλόχῳ φορέειν·
sentences.tr:
dōron toi kai egō, teknon phile, touto didōmi,
mnēm’ Helenēs cheirōn, polyēratou es gamou hōrēn,
sēi alochōi phoreein·
sentences.i: “I too give you this gift, dear child, a remembrance of Helen's hands, for the hour of your beloved marriage, for your wife to wear;
sentences.n: Helen answers the gift Menelaus has just given with one of her own. τοι is the dative 'you', and καὶ ἐγώ 'I too' points to Menelaus's gift. τέκνον φίλε is 'dear child': φίλε is the masculine vocative, though τέκνον is neuter. μνῆμα, 'memorial, remembrance', stands in apposition to δῶρον, and Helen names herself, Ἑλένης, so that the gift is 'of Helen's hands', her handiwork. πολυηράτου is 'much-loved', and ἐς γάμου ὥρην is 'for the hour of marriage'. σῇ ἀλόχῳ φορέειν is 'for your wife to wear': a dative of the person and an infinitive of purpose, φορέειν being the uncontracted form of φορεῖν.

sentences.t:
τῆος δὲ φίλῃ παρὰ μητρὶ
κείσθω ἐνὶ μεγάρῳ.
sentences.tr:
tēos de philēi para mētri
keisthō eni megarōi.
sentences.l:
and meanwhile beside (your) dear mother
let it lie in the hall.
sentences.i: and meanwhile let it lie in the hall beside your dear mother.
sentences.n: τῆος is 'meanwhile, for that time'. κείσθω is the third singular imperative of κεῖμαι 'lie'. φίλῃ παρὰ μητρί is 'beside a dear mother': the dative with παρά, and the Greek has no 'your', which the sense supplies. μέγαρον is here a singular, 'the hall'.

sentences.t:
σὺ δέ μοι χαίρων ἀφίκοιο
οἶκον ἐϋκτίμενον καὶ σὴν ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν.
sentences.tr:
sy de moi chairōn aphikoio
oikon eÿktimenon kai sēn es patrida gaian.
sentences.l:
and you, for me, rejoicing, may you arrive
at your well-built home and your own fatherland.”
sentences.i: And may you come rejoicing, as I wish, to your well-built home and your own native land.”
sentences.n: σὺ δέ μοι: μοι is a dative of interest, 'for me, as I wish'. ἀφίκοιο is the aorist optative of ἀφικνέομαι, 'may you arrive', a wish; χαίρων is 'rejoicing'. οἶκον is a bare accusative of the goal, with ἐς following for the second place. ἐϋκτίμενον 'well-built' is the house's epithet, translated every time. πατρίδα γαῖαν is 'fatherland', and σήν is the possessive 'your own'. The line also stands at 4.476 and 6.315, and its English is kept. The closing quotation mark ends Helen's speech.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰποῦσ’ ἐν χερσὶ τίθει, ὁ δ’ ἐδέξατο χαίρων.
sentences.tr: hōs eipous’ en chersi tithei, ho d’ edexato chairōn.
sentences.l: So having spoken, in his hands she placed it, and he received it, rejoicing.
sentences.i: So she spoke, and placed it in his hands, and he took it, rejoicing.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰποῦσ’ is the feminine of ὣς εἰπών at 120, 'so having spoken'. τίθει is again 'placed', and the object, the robe, is left to be understood. ὁ δ’ is 'and he', Telemachus; ἐδέξατο is the aorist middle of δέχομαι, 'received', and χαίρων 'rejoicing' echoes the word in Helen's wish at 128.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὰ μὲν ἐς πείρινθα τίθει Πεισίστρατος ἥρως
δεξάμενος, καὶ πάντα ἑῷ θηήσατο θυμῷ·
sentences.tr:
kai ta men es peirintha tithei Peisistratos hērōs
dexamenos, kai panta heōi thēēsato thymōi·
sentences.l:
And these into the chariot-basket placed Peisistratus the hero,
having received them, and everything he gazed at in wonder in his own heart;
sentences.i: Peisistratus the hero took them and stowed them in the chariot-basket, and he gazed at everything in wonder in his own heart;
sentences.n: τὰ μέν is 'these things', the gifts. πείρινθα is the accusative of πείρινς, the body or box of a vehicle, probably of plaited wicker; the word is rare, and the vehicle is the chariot of 145. τίθει is 'placed'. ἥρως 'hero' is kept with the name. δεξάμενος is the aorist middle participle 'having received'; the Greek does not say from whom. θηήσατο is the aorist of θηέομαι 'gaze at, wonder at', and ἑῷ is the possessive 'his own', not a pronoun 'him'; θυμῷ is 'heart'.

sentences.t: τοὺς δ’ ἦγε πρὸς δῶμα κάρη ξανθὸς Μενέλαος.
sentences.tr: tous d’ ēge pros dōma karē xanthos Menelaos.
sentences.l: and them led to the house, as to the head fair-haired, Menelaus.
sentences.i: and fair-haired Menelaus led them to the house.
sentences.n: τούς is 'them', the two young men, and ἦγε is 'led'. κάρη is the neuter noun 'head', standing beside ξανθός 'fair-haired', Menelaus's epithet, translated every time. It is most naturally an accusative of respect, 'fair as to the head', and the word-for-word English shows that; the construction is uncertain, and the readable English leaves it to ξανθός alone.

sentences.t: ἑζέσθην δ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα κατὰ κλισμούς τε θρόνους τε.
sentences.tr: hezesthēn d’ ar’ epeita kata klismous te thronous te.
sentences.l: And the two sat down then along the seats and the chairs.
sentences.i: Then the two of them sat down along the seats and the chairs.
sentences.n: ἑζέσθην is the dual of ἕζομαι 'seat oneself': 'the two sat down', Telemachus and Peisistratus, the same two as the dual νῶϊν at 168. κατά with the accusative is 'along'. κλισμούς are 'seats' and θρόνους 'chairs'; the half-line is a formula for settling guests.

sentences.t:
χέρνιβα δ’ ἀμφίπολος προχόῳ ἐπέχευε φέρουσα
καλῇ χρυσείῃ, ὑπὲρ ἀργυρέοιο λέβητος,
νίψασθαι·
sentences.tr:
cherniba d’ amphipolos prochoōi epecheue pherousa
kalēi chryseiēi, hyper argyreoio lebētos,
nipsasthai·
sentences.i: A handmaid brought water for the hands in a fine golden pitcher and poured it over a silver basin, for them to wash;
sentences.n: χέρνιβα is water for washing the hands. ἀμφίπολος is a female attendant, 'handmaid', and φέρουσα 'bringing' is a participle. προχόῳ is the dative of προχόος 'pitcher', and καλῇ χρυσείῃ is 'fine golden', both feminine datives. λέβητος, from λέβης, is the same word as the 'cauldron' of Menelaus's list of gifts at 15.84, in the previous part: a metal vessel, here the basin that catches the water. νίψασθαι is an aorist middle infinitive of purpose, 'to wash themselves'. The three lines are the standard hand-washing that precedes a meal.

sentences.t: παρὰ δὲ ξεστὴν ἐτάνυσσε τράπεζαν.
sentences.tr: para de xestēn etanysse trapezan.
sentences.l: and beside them she drew up a polished table.
sentences.i: and she drew a polished table up beside them.
sentences.n: παρὰ δέ is 'and beside', with παρά an adverb. ξεστήν 'polished' is from ξέω 'plane, scrape smooth'. ἐτάνυσσε is the aorist of τανύω 'stretch', here 'draw up'. The subject is still the handmaid. The line is shipped word for word at 2.138, and the English is kept.

sentences.t: σῖτον δ’ αἰδοίη ταμίη παρέθηκε φέρουσα·
sentences.tr: siton d’ aidoiē tamiē parethēke pherousa·
sentences.l: And bread a revered housekeeper set beside them, bringing it;
sentences.i: A revered housekeeper brought bread and set it beside them;
sentences.n: σῖτον is 'bread, food'. αἰδοίη ταμίη is 'a revered housekeeper', the standing phrase, translated every time. παρέθηκε is the aorist of παρατίθημι 'set beside', and φέρουσα is the participle 'bringing'. The line ends at an ano teleia, and the next line goes on with what she did.

sentences.t: εἴδατα πόλλ’ ἐπιθεῖσα, χαριζομένη παρεόντων·
sentences.tr: eidata poll’ epitheisa, charizomenē pareontōn·
sentences.l: and laid on many dishes, giving freely of what was at hand;
sentences.i: and laid on many dishes, giving freely of what she had by her;
sentences.n: ἐπιθεῖσα is the aorist participle of ἐπιτίθημι 'lay on'. εἴδατα are 'dishes, foods', and πόλλ’ is πολλά 'many'. χαριζομένη is 'giving freely, favouring', and παρεόντων is a partitive genitive, 'of what was at hand'.

sentences.t: πὰρ δὲ Βοηθοΐδης κρέα δαίετο καὶ νέμε μοίρας·
sentences.tr: par de Boēthoïdēs krea daieto kai neme moiras·
sentences.l: and beside them the son of Boethous was carving the meats and distributing portions;
sentences.i: and beside them the son of Boethous carved the meat and handed round the portions;
sentences.n: πάρ is παρά 'beside'. Βοηθοΐδης is the patronymic of 95, 'the son of Boethous', now standing alone for Eteoneus. δαίετο is the imperfect middle of δαίομαι 'divide, carve', and νέμε is the unaugmented imperfect of νέμω 'distribute'. μοίρας are 'portions'.

sentences.t: οἰνοχόει δ’ υἱὸς Μενελάου κυδαλίμοιο.
sentences.tr: oinochoei d’ huios Menelaou kydalimoio.
sentences.l: And the son of Menelaus, glorious, was pouring wine.
sentences.i: and the son of glorious Menelaus poured the wine.
sentences.n: οἰνοχόει is the imperfect of οἰνοχοέω 'pour wine'. υἱὸς Μενελάου κυδαλίμοιο is 'the son of Menelaus, glorious': κυδαλίμοιο is a genitive in -οιο, an epithet translated every time. The son is not named here, but the only son of Menelaus named in this part is Megapenthes (100, 103, 122), the likely meaning.

sentences.t: οἱ δ’ ἐπ’ ὀνείαθ’ ἑτοῖμα προκείμενα χεῖρας ἴαλλον.
sentences.tr: hoi d’ ep’ oneiath’ hetoima prokeimena cheiras iallon.
sentences.l: And they to the good things ready and set before them put out their hands.
sentences.i: And they put out their hands to the good things lying ready before them.
sentences.n: ὀνείαθ’ is 'good things, things to enjoy', ἑτοῖμα is 'ready' and προκείμενα is 'lying before them', all neuter plurals in agreement. χεῖρας ἴαλλον is 'put out their hands', a formula for beginning a meal, with ἴαλλον the imperfect of ἰάλλω 'send, stretch out'.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ πόσιος καὶ ἐδητύος ἐξ ἔρον ἕντο,
δὴ τότε Τηλέμαχος καὶ Νέστορος ἀγλαὸς υἱὸς
ἵππους τε ζεύγνυντ’ ἀνά θ’ ἅρματα ποικίλ’ ἔβαινον,
ἐκ δ’ ἔλασαν προθύροιο καὶ αἰθούσης ἐριδούπου.
sentences.tr:
autar epei posios kai edētyos ex eron hento,
dē tote Tēlemachos kai Nestoros aglaos huios
hippous te zeugnynt’ ana th’ harmata poikil’ ebainon,
ek d’ elasan prothyroio kai aithousēs eridoupou.
sentences.l:
But when of drink and of food they had put away desire,
then indeed Telemachus and Nestor's splendid son
both the horses they yoked, and up onto the inlaid chariot they stepped,
and out they drove from the forecourt and the loud-echoing portico.
sentences.i: But when they had put from them the desire for drink and food, Telemachus and Nestor's splendid son yoked the horses and mounted the inlaid chariot, and drove out of the forecourt and the loud-echoing portico.
sentences.n: The sentence opens with the formula that ends a meal: ἔρον ἕντο is 'put away desire', where ἕντο is an aorist middle of ἵημι 'send' and ἐξ is tmesis for it. ἀγλαός is 'splendid'; in Νέστορος ἀγλαὸς υἱός the Greek gives Peisistratus no name, only his father's. ζεύγνυντ’ is the elided imperfect middle of ζεύγνυμι 'yoke'. ἀνά … ἔβαινον is tmesis for ἀνέβαινον 'mounted', and ποικίλ’ is 'inlaid'. ἔλασαν is the aorist of ἐλαύνω 'drive'. προθύροιο is a genitive of the place left, going with ἐκ … ἔλασαν, 'out of the forecourt', and αἰθούσης ἐριδούπου is 'the loud-echoing portico'.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δὲ μετ’ Ἀτρεΐδης ἔκιε ξανθὸς Μενέλαος,
οἶνον ἔχων ἐν χειρὶ μελίφρονα δεξιτερῆφι,
ἐν δέπαϊ χρυσέῳ, ὄφρα λείψαντε κιοίτην.
sentences.tr:
tous de met’ Atreïdēs ekie xanthos Menelaos,
oinon echōn en cheiri meliphrona dexiterēphi,
en depaï chryseōi, ophra leipsante kioitēn.
sentences.l:
And after them went the son of Atreus, fair-haired Menelaus,
wine holding in his hand, honey-hearted, in the right,
in a golden cup, so that, having poured a libation, the two might go.
sentences.i: Behind them came the son of Atreus, fair-haired Menelaus, holding heart-sweetening wine in his right hand, in a golden cup, so that the two of them might pour a libation before they went.
sentences.n: τοὺς δὲ μετ’ is 'and after them'. ἔκιε is the imperfect of κίω 'go'. Ἀτρεΐδης used alone is 'the son of Atreus', and ξανθός 'fair-haired' is again translated. μελίφρονα is 'honey-hearted', that is 'heart-sweetening'; the sense of the compound is uncertain, and the first part, μέλι 'honey', is clear. δεξιτερῆφι has the ending -φι, here 'in the right (hand)'. δέπαϊ is the dative of δέπας, and χρυσέῳ is 'golden'. ὄφρα with the optative κιοίτην, a dual, is 'so that the two might go'; λείψαντε is a dual aorist participle, taken as from λείβω 'pour', so 'having poured a libation', the object being left understood.

sentences.t: στῆ δ’ ἵππων προπάροιθε, δεδισκόμενος δὲ προσηύδα·
sentences.tr: stē d’ hippōn proparoithe, dediskomenos de prosēuda·
sentences.l: And he stood before the horses, and in greeting he spoke:
sentences.i: He stopped in front of the horses and spoke in greeting:
sentences.n: στῆ is the unaugmented aorist of ἵστημι, 'stood', and ἵππων προπάροιθε is 'before the horses'. δεδισκόμενος is a participle of a rare verb meaning 'greet' or 'pledge'; its exact sense is not certain, and 'greeting' is the traditional reading, suited to the cup in his hand. προσηύδα is 'spoke to', and the Greek leaves the two young men to be understood.

sentences.t:
χαίρετον, ὦ κούρω, καὶ Νέστορι ποιμένι λαῶν
εἰπεῖν·
sentences.tr:
chaireton, ō kourō, kai Nestori poimeni laōn
eipein·
sentences.l:
“Be glad, O two youths, and to Nestor, shepherd of the people,
to tell it;
sentences.i: “Fare well, young men, and tell Nestor, shepherd of the people, the same;
sentences.n: Menelaus is speaking to the two young men, so χαίρετον is a dual imperative, 'be glad', which is the parting word 'fare well'; ὦ κούρω is a dual vocative, 'O two youths'. καὶ Νέστορι ποιμένι λαῶν is 'and to Nestor, shepherd of the people', the standing phrase, translated every time. εἰπεῖν is an infinitive standing for a command, with no object stated: the thing to be told Nestor is the same farewell. The ano teleia ends the unit, and ἦ γάρ opens the reason.

sentences.t:
ἦ γὰρ ἐμοί γε πατὴρ ὣς ἤπιος ἦεν,
ἧος ἐνὶ Τροίῃ πολεμίζομεν υἷες Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
ē gar emoi ge patēr hōs ēpios ēen,
hēos eni Troiēi polemizomen huies Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
for truly to me, at least, like a father kind he was,
while in Troy we fought, the sons of the Achaeans.”
sentences.i: for he was as gentle to me as a father, while we, the sons of the Achaeans, fought at Troy.”
sentences.n: ἦ γάρ is 'for truly', and ἐμοί γε 'to me, at least'. πατὴρ ὣς ἤπιος ἦεν is 'was gentle as a father': ὥς with the accent is 'as', and ἦεν is the epic form of ἦν. The subject is Nestor, understood from the previous unit. ἧος is the epic ἕως 'while', and πολεμίζομεν is an imperfect without the augment. Τροίῃ has Ionic η, and υἷες is the epic nominative plural 'sons'; υἷες Ἀχαιῶν is a fixed periphrasis for the Achaean fighting men, here including Menelaus himself. The closing quotation mark ends Menelaus's speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.tr: ton d’ au Tēlemachos pepnymenos antion ēuda·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: The same formula as at 86, the fixed introduction to Telemachus's replies; the English is the same. τόν is Menelaus, and πεπνυμένος 'prudent' is translated every time.

sentences.t:
καὶ λίην κείνῳ γε, διοτρεφές, ὡς ἀγορεύεις,
πάντα τάδ’ ἐλθόντες καταλέξομεν·
sentences.tr:
kai liēn keinōi ge, diotrephes, hōs agoreueis,
panta tad’ elthontes katalexomen·
sentences.l:
“And very much so, to him at least, Zeus-nurtured one, as you declare,
all this, having come, we shall recount;
sentences.i: “Yes, quite so, Zeus-nurtured one, as you say; when we have come we shall tell him all of this;
sentences.n: καὶ λίην is 'yes, very much so', agreeing with Menelaus. κείνῳ is the epic dative 'to him' (Attic ἐκείνῳ), Nestor, and γε emphasises it. διοτρεφές is the vocative 'Zeus-nurtured one', as at 87. ὡς ἀγορεύεις is 'as you declare', put in as a parenthesis. ἐλθόντες is the aorist participle 'having come', and καταλέξομεν is the future of καταλέγω 'recount in full'. The ano teleia ends the unit; αἲ γάρ begins a wish.

sentences.t:
αἲ γὰρ ἐγὼν ὣς
νοστήσας Ἰθάκηνδε, κιχὼν Ὀδυσῆ’ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ,
εἴποιμ’ ὡς παρὰ σεῖο τυχὼν φιλότητος ἁπάσης
ἔρχομαι, αὐτὰρ ἄγω κειμήλια πολλὰ καὶ ἐσθλά.
sentences.tr:
ai gar egōn hōs
nostēsas Ithakēnde, kichōn Odysē’ eni oikōi,
eipoim’ hōs para seio tychōn philotētos hapasēs
erchomai, autar agō keimēlia polla kai esthla.
sentences.l:
Would that I, just so,
having come home to Ithaca, having found Odysseus in the house,
might tell how, from you having met with all friendship,
I come, and I bring many treasures, and good ones.”
sentences.i: if only I might reach Ithaca in this way, find Odysseus in the house, and tell him how I come, having met with every kindness from you, and how I bring many treasures, and good ones.”
sentences.n: αἲ γάρ opens a wish, 'if only'. ἐγών is the epic form of ἐγώ. ὣς is 'so, thus'; it goes most naturally with νοστήσας, 'returning in this way', that is, so favoured, but the Greek does not say what it points back to. νοστήσας is the aorist participle of νοστέω 'return home', Ἰθάκηνδε is 'to Ithaca' (-δε of direction), κιχών is the aorist participle of κιχάνω 'find', and Ὀδυσῆ’ is the elided accusative Ὀδυσῆα. εἴποιμ’ is the optative of the wish, and ὡς with ἔρχομαι and ἄγω is 'how I come … how I bring', both in the present. σεῖο is the epic genitive of σύ, and τυχών with a genitive is 'having met with, obtained'; φιλότητος ἁπάσης is 'all friendship, every kindness'. κειμήλια πολλὰ καὶ ἐσθλά is 'many treasures, and good ones'. The closing quotation mark ends Telemachus's speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα οἱ εἰπόντι ἐπέπτατο δεξιὸς ὄρνις,
αἰετὸς ἀργὴν χῆνα φέρων ὀνύχεσσι πέλωρον,
ἥμερον ἐξ αὐλῆς·
sentences.tr:
hōs ara hoi eiponti epeptato dexios ornis,
aietos argēn chēna pherōn onychessi pelōron,
hēmeron ex aulēs·
sentences.i: As soon as he had spoken, a bird flew up on the right, an eagle carrying in its talons a huge white goose, a tame one from the yard;
sentences.n: An omen. οἱ εἰπόντι is 'to him having spoken', a dative of the speaker, 'just as he spoke'; ἐπέπτατο is the aorist middle of ἐπιπέτομαι 'fly up to'. δεξιός is 'on the right', the lucky side, as the joy at 164–165 shows. αἰετός is the Ionic form of ἀετός 'eagle'. ἀργήν is 'white': ἀργός means 'bright, white' and also 'swift', and for a goose 'white' is the plain sense. φέρων ὀνύχεσσι is 'carrying in its talons', a dative plural in -εσσι. πέλωρον is 'huge', related to the noun πέλωρ 'monster', and ἥμερον is 'tame'; both agree with χῆνα. αὐλή is an enclosed yard.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἰΰζοντες ἕποντο
ἀνέρες ἠδὲ γυναῖκες·
sentences.tr:
hoi d’ iÿzontes heponto
aneres ēde gynaikes·
sentences.l:
and they, shouting, followed,
men and women;
sentences.i: and men and women followed it, shouting;
sentences.n: οἱ is the pronoun 'they', and ἀνέρες ἠδὲ γυναῖκες 'men and women' explains it; ἀνέρες is the epic nominative plural of ἀνήρ. ἰΰζοντες is a participle of ἰΰζω 'cry out', a loud shout. ἕποντο is the unaugmented imperfect of ἕπομαι 'follow', here 'followed it'.

sentences.t:
ὁ δέ σφισιν ἐγγύθεν ἐλθὼν
δεξιὸς ἤϊξε πρόσθ’ ἵππων·
sentences.tr:
ho de sphisin engythen elthōn
dexios ēïxe prosth’ hippōn·
sentences.l:
and it, to them from near having come,
on the right darted in front of the horses;
sentences.i: and it came close to them and darted in front of the horses, on the right;
sentences.n: ὁ δέ is 'but it', the eagle. σφισιν is the epic dative plural 'to them', and ἐγγύθεν is 'from near' (-θεν 'from'), here 'close up'. δεξιός is 'on the right' again; ἤϊξε is the aorist of ἀΐσσω 'dart'. πρόσθ’ ἵππων is 'before the horses', πρόσθε with the genitive.

sentences.t:
οἱ δὲ ἰδόντες
γήθησαν, καὶ πᾶσιν ἐνὶ φρεσὶ θυμὸς ἰάνθη.
sentences.tr:
hoi de idontes
gēthēsan, kai pasin eni phresi thymos ianthē.
sentences.l:
and they, having seen it,
rejoiced, and for all in their minds the heart was warmed.
sentences.i: and when they saw it they rejoiced, and the heart was cheered in all their minds.
sentences.n: οἱ δὲ ἰδόντες is 'and they, having seen', the aorist participle of εἶδον; the object, the eagle, is left unsaid. γήθησαν is the aorist of γηθέω 'rejoice'. πᾶσιν ἐνὶ φρεσί is 'in the minds of all'; θυμός is 'heart', and ἰάνθη is the aorist passive of ἰαίνω 'warm, cheer'. Their joy shows that the bird on the right counts as a good sign.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ Νεστορίδης Πεισίστρατος ἤρχετο μύθων·
sentences.tr: toisi de Nestoridēs Peisistratos ērcheto mythōn·
sentences.l: And among them of speeches began Nestor's son, Peisistratus:
sentences.i: Peisistratus, son of Nestor, was the first to speak among them:
sentences.n: τοῖσι is the dative 'among them'. Νεστορίδης is a patronymic, 'son of Nestor', standing beside the man's own name. ἤρχετο is the imperfect middle of ἄρχω, which with the genitive μύθων means 'begin the speeches'; the line is a whole-line speech introduction.

sentences.t:
φράζεο δή, Μενέλαε διοτρεφές, ὄρχαμε λαῶν,
ἢ νῶϊν τόδ’ ἔφηνε θεὸς τέρας ἦε σοὶ αὐτῷ.
sentences.tr:
phrazeo dē, Menelae diotrephes, orchame laōn,
ē nōïn tod’ ephēne theos teras ēe soi autōi.
sentences.l:
“Consider now, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, chief of the people,
whether to us two this portent a god showed, or to you yourself.”
sentences.i: “Consider now, Menelaus, Zeus-nurtured, chief of the people, whether a god has shown this portent to the two of us, or to you yourself.”
sentences.n: φράζεο is the second singular imperative of φράζομαι 'consider, ponder', and δή is 'now'. Μενέλαε διοτρεφές, ὄρχαμε λαῶν is the address of 87 without the patronymic, translated the same. ἢ … ἦε is 'whether … or', ἦε being the epic form of ἠέ 'or', a double indirect question. νῶϊν is the dual dative 'to us two'. ἔφηνε is the aorist of φαίνω 'show', and τέρας is a 'portent, marvel'. σοὶ αὐτῷ is 'to you yourself'. The closing quotation mark ends Peisistratus's speech.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, μερμήριξε δ’ ἀρηΐφιλος Μενέλαος,
ὅππως οἱ κατὰ μοῖραν ὑποκρίναιτο νοήσας.
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, mermērixe d’ arēïphilos Menelaos,
hoppōs hoi kata moiran hypokrinaito noēsas.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and pondered Ares-loved Menelaus,
how to him according to what is fitting he might answer, having thought it over.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Menelaus, dear to Ares, pondered how he might, once he had thought it over, answer him as is fitting.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is 'So he spoke', the stock formula. μερμήριξε is the aorist of μερμηρίζω 'be in two minds, ponder'. ἀρηΐφιλος is another epithet of Menelaus, 'dear to Ares', translated every time: φίλος can be passive, 'dear to', or active, 'loving'; 'dear to Ares' is the usual reading. ὅππως is ὅπως 'how', and ὑποκρίναιτο is the aorist optative middle of ὑποκρίνομαι 'answer'; here the answer is an interpretation of the portent. οἱ is the dative 'to him', Peisistratus, and κατὰ μοῖραν is 'as is fitting'. νοήσας is the aorist participle of νοέω 'think, consider'.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ Ἑλένη τανύπεπλος ὑποφθαμένη φάτο μῦθον·
sentences.tr: ton d’ Helenē tanypeplos hypophthamenē phato mython·
sentences.l: And him Helen, long-robed, forestalling, spoke a speech:
sentences.i: And long-robed Helen, getting in before him, spoke:
sentences.n: τόν is Menelaus, the man who is still deliberating, and it is the object of ὑποφθαμένη, 'getting ahead of him' (ὑποφθάνω 'forestall, anticipate'). τανύπεπλος 'long-robed' is Helen's epithet, translated every time. φάτο is the unaugmented aorist middle of φημί 'say', and μῦθον, its object, is 'a speech'. Helen's speech follows in the next part, and its opening quotation mark is printed there.
